betterCitation: Mark Twain, The Mysterious Stranger, ch. 10 (Satan) (Paine and Duneka text, Harper and Brothers, 1916)
reason:
Three independent readings this run, and the wording, the locator and the speaker all hold. Wikisource's transcription of chapter 10, which states on its index page that it is the 1916 Paine-Duneka text, prints: 'Power, money, persuasion, supplication, persecution--these can lift at a colossal humbug--push it a little--weaken it a little, century by century; but only laughter can blow it to rags and atoms at a blast. Against the assault of laughter nothing can stand.' Satan is speaking, and the chapter opens 'Days and days went by now, and no Satan.' The WIST quotation entry gives the same sentence with the same lowercase 'laughter', cites it as The Mysterious Stranger, ch. 10 (1916), and names Satan as the speaker. A third reading agreed on ch. 10. The shipped sentence is verbatim: 'Against the assault of laughter nothing can stand.' The CFL candidate list carries it with a comma after 'laughter'; the verifier correctly dropped that comma, because the 1916 text has none. That is the citation working as intended.

THE CAPITALISATION TRAP, AND WHY IT LANDS ON THE RIGHT SIDE. There are two texts of this speech and they differ in exactly the way that would sink a careless citation. Twain's own manuscript, The Chronicle of Young Satan (c. 1898, published in Mark Twain's Mysterious Stranger Manuscripts, ed. Tuckey, 1969), capitalises the personifications: 'Power, Money, Persuasion, Supplication, Persecution' and 'but only Laughter can blow it to rags and atoms at a blast', and WIST records that variant separately. The 1916 Harper text lowercases them. The proposal ships lowercase and names the 1916 Harper text, so the wording and the named edition agree. Had it shipped lowercase while citing the manuscript, or capital L while citing 1916, I would have refuted. It does neither.

THE ONE THING I WOULD CHANGE, AND IT IS NOT FATAL. The 1916 Mysterious Stranger is not a book Twain finished or authorised. Albert Bigelow Paine and Frederick Duneka assembled it after his death out of the Mysterious Stranger manuscripts, renamed a character, and grafted on an ending taken from a different manuscript altogether; Tuckey's work in the 1960s is why the Mark Twain Papers no longer treat it as Twain's text. That matters here less than it usually does, because the laughter speech is NOT one of the editors' inventions: it stands in Twain's own Chronicle of Young Satan, in that manuscript's chapter 10 as well, which is why WIST can print both versions side by side. So the attribution to Twain is sound and the citation is honest: it names the edition, and the wording is that edition's. But the note field is empty, and a card citing a posthumously assembled text ought to say so somewhere. Two fixes, either of which suffices. The cheap one is the source line I put in betterCitation, 102 characters, which flags the Paine and Duneka text on the card itself. The better one is a note along the lines that the 1916 Harper text was assembled after Twain's death by Paine and Duneka, and that this speech is Twain's own, standing in his Chronicle of Young Satan manuscript with Laughter capitalised. I did not refute on the empty note because rule 12's bar is a confident FALSE citation, and nothing in this citation is false.

EVERY OTHER GATE. shipped.js on the exact line: shipped [], near [], person resolves to samuel clemens at 0 of 3 for the year, cap 3, not banned. Nothing on the misattribution list touches it; the Twain entry there is 'Dance like nobody's watching', which is a 1987 Clark and Leigh lyric and not this. Speaker named: '(Satan)' after the locator, which is what rule 5 requires for a character's line, and it is the right character, the visiting angel who calls himself Satan, not the fallen one. Scope: 1916, a novella, not scripture, film, lyric, proverb, business or oratory, and well before 1999. Publishable: the speech is about humbug and laughter and describes no wound or dying; the surrounding chapter is darker than the line, but the line as printed needs no warning. Source line is 79 characters, leads with the author's name, carries no dash, and the doubled parentheses are the pattern the carry already ships (compare the Fleming and Tolkien carry-ins, which put speaker and publisher in adjacent parentheses in either order). Tag Fiction is the form of the work. Theme fit is honest: laughter as the one effective weapon a poor race owns is courage under trial rather than cheer, and it reads well at six in the morning.
